q: What does the Scope performance domain ensure?
options: That the project finishes within the approved budget
That every single stakeholder request is added to the project scope
All the work required is included, and no unnecessary work
That the schedule baseline is never changed during work
explanation: The Scope performance domain includes the processes required to ensure the project encompasses all of the work required, and that no unnecessary work is performed, to maximize the project's value.

q: What is a requirement, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: A condition or capability needed to satisfy a business need
Any feature a stakeholder would like to have in the product
A task assigned to a team member in the project schedule
A constraint imposed on the project by the sponsor's budget
explanation: A requirement is a condition or capability that is necessary to be present in a product, service or result to satisfy a business need.

q: Before requirements are baselined, which quality must they have?
options: Written only by the sponsor
Approved by every end user
Ordered by cost, lowest first
Measurable and testable
explanation: Before being baselined, requirements should be unambiguous (measurable and testable), traceable, complete, consistent and acceptable to key stakeholders.

q: Why use a requirements traceability matrix?
options: To assign each of the requirements to an external vendor for pricing
To link each requirement from its origin to its deliverable
To record the hours spent on each requirement
To replace the need for acceptance criteria
explanation: The matrix links product requirements from their origin to the deliverables that satisfy them and to the business and project objectives, so each requirement adds value and approved requirements are delivered.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Requirements traceability matrix

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Requirements traceability matrix

q: The requirements traceability matrix is shown. What should the project manager do about R2 before the deliverable is accepted?
options: Remove R2, since it already has a design
Accept R2 because it links to a business objective
Make sure R2 is tested before acceptance is sought
Move R2 to the next phase without telling anyone
explanation: R2 traces to an objective and a design but has no test. Requirements must be testable, and the matrix helps ensure that approved requirements are delivered; R2 needs a test before its deliverable can be verified and accepted.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Requirements traceability matrix

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Requirements traceability matrix

q: Which content does the project scope statement include?
options: Major deliverables, assumptions, constraints and exclusions
The cost baseline and the funding requirements
The names and salaries of the project team members
The risk register together with the planned response for each single risk
explanation: The project scope statement describes the project scope, major deliverables, assumptions and constraints, and acceptance criteria; it may contain explicit exclusions.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Project scope statement

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Project scope statement

q: Why might a scope statement list explicit exclusions?
options: To make the contract longer and more formal
To allow the team to skip quality checks
To reduce the number of stakeholders involved
To help manage stakeholder expectations
explanation: The project scope statement may contain explicit scope exclusions that can assist in managing stakeholder expectations.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Project scope statement

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Project scope statement

q: In an adaptive environment, in what form are requirements usually collected?
options: As a fixed list signed off before any work
As user stories prioritized in a backlog
As work packages in a detailed WBS
As clauses in the final contract
explanation: In an adaptive environment, the requirements are collected in the form of user stories that are then prioritized in a backlog.

q: How is the product backlog broken down in agile projects, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: Into work packages, then activities
Into phases, then control accounts
Into epics, features and user stories
Into tasks assigned by the project manager
explanation: In agile projects, Develop Scope Structure corresponds to product backlog breakdown, where work items are broken down into epics, features and user stories.

q: What is a work package?
options: The lowest WBS level, where cost and duration are estimated
The highest level of the WBS, which shows the whole of the project
A contract package sent to suppliers for bidding
A set of documents handed over at project closure
explanation: The work package is the work defined at the lowest level of the WBS for which cost and duration can be estimated and managed.

q: A team's WBS leaves out all the project management work. Which principle does this break?
options: Rolling wave planning
Progressive elaboration
The definition of done
The 100 percent rule
explanation: The WBS represents all product and project work, including the project management work; the work at the lowest levels rolls up so that nothing is left out and no extra work is performed: the 100 percent rule.

q: A deliverable will only be built in two years and its details are not yet agreed. How should it appear in the WBS now?
options: Decomposed fully now, using assumptions
At a high level, decomposed later when agreed
Left out of the WBS entirely until work on it begins
Assigned to the sponsor to define alone
explanation: Decomposition may not be possible for a deliverable far in the future; the team waits until it is agreed before developing the WBS details. This is rolling wave planning.

q: Which information does the WBS dictionary provide?
options: The overall budget for the project and the full funding plan for it
The sponsor's signature on the business case
Details such as responsible parties and acceptance criteria
The stakeholder register's classification data
explanation: The WBS dictionary provides additional detail about each WBS component, such as scope descriptions, milestones, responsible parties, resource needs and acceptance criteria.

q: Which process produces verified deliverables?
options: Monitor and Control Scope
Validate Scope
Define Scope
Develop Scope Structure
explanation: Verified deliverables are checked and confirmed for correctness through Monitor and Control Scope; they then become an input to Validate Scope for formal acceptance.

q: What is the main purpose of the Validate Scope process?
options: To check that deliverables are correct before quality control
To formalize acceptance of the completed deliverables
To create the WBS and the WBS dictionary
To estimate the cost of each work package
explanation: Validate Scope checks the processes used to achieve quality standards and formalizes acceptance of the deliverables, increasing the probability of acceptance.

q: In which order do deliverables usually move through these steps?
options: Accepted, then verified, then built
Validated by the customer first, and then quality-checked
Accepted by the sponsor before any inspection
Verified for correctness, then formally accepted
explanation: Monitor and Control Scope produces verified deliverables, checked for correctness; these are inputs to Validate Scope, which produces accepted deliverables.

q: In an adaptive approach, when is the scope baseline defined, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: At the beginning of each iteration
Once, before the first iteration
Only at the final release
When the supplier contract is signed at the start
explanation: For adaptive approaches, the baseline is defined at the beginning of each iteration, aligned with the prioritized requirements based on the value expected.

q: In an adaptive environment, who usually approves changes to scope, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: The change control board
The sponsor alone
The product owner
The functional manager
explanation: In adaptive environments it is usually a product owner who dynamically approves changes, in a more flexible environment without a formal change control procedure.

q: A developer adds an extra report the customer never asked for, hoping to impress them. What is this called?
options: Scope creep
Rolling wave planning
Decomposition
Gold plating
explanation: Adding features nobody asked for is gold plating. A value-focused approach uses continuous scope management to prevent scope creep and gold plating.

q: A stakeholder informally asks a team member to add a small feature to a predictive project. What should happen?
options: The team member adds it, since it is small
It goes through change control against the scope baseline
The project manager refuses every change request during execution
The feature is added and reported at closure
explanation: Monitor and Control Scope manages changes to the scope baseline; the baseline can be changed only through formal change control. Adding unapproved work is scope creep.

q: According to the PMBOK Guide, how does quality relate to scope?
options: Quality is an integral attribute of scope
Quality is separate and handled after scope
Quality only matters for adaptive projects
Quality is the sponsor's concern, not the team's
explanation: Quality is an integral attribute of scope, including functional and nonfunctional requirements; a bridge's scope includes thresholds for how sturdy, long-lasting and maintainable it is.

q: What does a value breakdown structure add to the scope?
options: A planned schedule date for every work package
A responsible person for each deliverable
A value estimate for each major deliverable
The procurement method for each component
explanation: A VBS connects scope to its intended value: each major deliverable carries a value-based number or a percentage of the total value (100% if mandatory), used to prioritize deliverables and work.

q: What is the definition of done in an adaptive approach?
options: The date on which the project must be finished
Shared criteria a story or increment must meet to be complete
The sponsor's signature on each final deliverable at the very end
A list of all the user stories in the backlog
explanation: In adaptive approaches, the DoD is a shared understanding of the criteria that should be met before a piece of work, such as a user story, feature or increment, is complete and ready for release.

q: When should the stakeholder who will accept the deliverables get involved, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: Only at the final acceptance meeting
Only after all of the deliverables have been verified by the team
Only if a change request is raised
Early, giving feedback on quality as work proceeds
explanation: The authorized stakeholder who approves the deliverables should get involved early and provide feedback on quality, so the team can assess quality and performance and recommend changes.

q: A project relies on several subcontractors. What does the PMBOK Guide advise about scope?
options: Keep scope out of the contracts to stay flexible
Let each subcontractor define its own part of the scope entirely alone
Integrate scope into the contracts early, synchronizing commitments
Define scope only after all contracts have been signed
explanation: With external partners, deciding how to integrate scope into contractual agreements is critical; early alignment sets expectations, and all parties' scope-related commitments must be synchronized.

q: Which THREE qualities should requirements have before they are baselined?
options: Measurable and testable
Traceable
Consistent
Written by the sponsor alone
Ordered by cost
Free of any assumptions
explanation: Before being baselined, requirements should be unambiguous (measurable and testable), traceable, complete, consistent and acceptable to key stakeholders.

q: Which TWO are tools and techniques of the Elicit and Analyze Requirements process?
options: Focus groups
Interviews
Earned value analysis
Critical path method
Make-or-buy analysis
explanation: Figure 2-15 lists expert judgment, decision-making, benchmarking, brainstorming, focus groups, interviews, questionnaires and surveys, document analysis, nominal group, design thinking, prioritization and meetings.

q: Which TWO describe scope in agile projects, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: Often represented at a high level by a product roadmap
Defined progressively through a backlog
Fully fixed in a WBS before the first iteration
Changed only through a change control board
Owned by the functional manager
explanation: In agile projects scope is typically considered at a high level, often represented by the product roadmap and its releases, and deliverables are progressively defined through a backlog.

q: Match each scope process with what it does.
right: Creates the plan for defining, controlling and validating scope
Describes the project and product, with quality requirements
Formalizes acceptance of the completed deliverables
explanation: The six Scope processes are Plan Scope Management, Elicit and Analyze Requirements, Define Scope, Develop Scope Structure, Monitor and Control Scope, and Validate Scope.

q: Complete each statement with the scope process where it happens.

blanks.text: Stakeholders' needs are first determined and documented in
Deliverables are checked for correctness in

explanation: Requirements are elicited and analyzed, deliverables are verified in Monitor and Control Scope, and Validate Scope formalizes their acceptance.
